move.title: Rub it in, cook it slow
move.body: Welsh cakes are little sweet cakes from Wales, cooked on a griddle instead of in the oven. Today you'll rub cold butter into flour with your fingertips, roll and cut the dough, and cook the cakes slowly in a skillet until golden on both sides.

callback.body: Biscuits used cold butter in pieces for flaky layers. Welsh cakes rub the butter in smaller, like breadcrumbs, so they come out tender and soft instead of flaky.

why.title: Rubbing in
why.body: Rubbing cold butter into flour with your fingertips coats the flour in fat. Coated flour can't make much gluten, so the cakes are tender, not chewy.

why.title: Keep it cold
why.body: Cold butter rubs in as crumbs. Warm butter turns greasy and sticky. Use just your fingertips, which are cooler than your palms.

why.title: Low and slow
why.body: The cakes are thick and full of sugar. On high heat the outside burns before the middle cooks. Medium-low heat browns them gently while the inside cooks through.

wrong.fix: The butter got warm. Put the bowl in the fridge for 10 minutes.

wrong.sign: The dough is too dry to hold together
wrong.fix: Add milk a teaspoon at a time.

wrong.sign: The outside is dark but the middle is doughy
wrong.fix: Turn the heat lower and cook the next ones a minute longer on each side.
Turn the heat up a little and cook 1 more minute.

quiz.q: What does rubbing butter into flour do?
choices: Coats the flour so the cakes stay tender
They're cooler, so the butter stays cold

quiz.q: Why cook Welsh cakes on medium-low heat?
choices: So the middle cooks before the outside burns

ingredients.text: a little more, for the pan

substitutions.note: Chop big raisins in half with the butter knife.

steps.text: Cut the cold butter into small cubes with the butter knife. Put them on the plate in the fridge.
steps.tip: Measure everything else while it chills.

steps.text: Spoon and level the flour into the large bowl. Whisk in the ⅓ cup of sugar, baking powder, salt, and cinnamon.
Add the butter. Rub it into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs.
steps.look: Fine crumbs, with no big lumps of butter.
steps.tip: Lift the crumbs and let them fall as you rub. It keeps them cool.

steps.text: Beat the egg and milk in the small bowl with the fork. Pour it into the crumbs and stir.
steps.look: A soft dough that holds together.
steps.tip: Don't taste the raw dough. It has raw egg.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and throw away the eggshell.
Flour the counter. Roll the dough out ¼ inch thick.
steps.tip: About as thick as two stacked quarters.

steps.text: Press the cutter straight down to cut rounds. Press the scraps together and roll them once more.
Heat the skillet over medium-low heat. Rub it with a little butter on a paper towel.
Lay 6 cakes in the pan. Cook until the bottoms are golden brown.
Flip them with the spatula. Cook the other side.
Break the first cake open. It should be cooked through, with no wet dough.

target.look: Cooked through in the middle, golden on both sides

steps.tip: Doughy? Turn the heat lower and cook the rest longer.

steps.text: Move the cakes to the rack and sprinkle them with sugar. Cook the rest the same way, then turn off the stove.
steps.tip: Sugar sticks best while they are warm.
